business.what_it_does: Website analytics software that tracks site visitors (pageviews, sources, campaigns, events and revenue) without cookies or tracking visitors' personal data.

facts.statement: Fathom automatically and intelligently routes data from EU visitors to be processed in the EU and all other visitors to be processed in the US.

provenance.quote: Fathom automatically and intelligently routes data from EU visitors to be processed in the EU and all other visitors to be processed in the US.

facts.statement: If you need more than the sites included in a plan, you can add up to 15 packs of 50 extra sites from billing settings, at $10/month or $100/year per pack.

provenance.quote: If you need more, you can add up to 15 packs of 50 extra sites yourself from your billing settings, at $10/month or $100/year per pack.

facts.statement: Sites on the same plan share that plan's monthly pageview allotment.

provenance.quote: Sites on a plan share your monthly pageviews. The larger pageview plans include more sites, and you can add extra site packs from billing if you need them.

facts.statement: Fathom retains a customer's analytics data indefinitely for as long as they remain a customer.

provenance.quote: How long do you store my analytics data? Forever, as long as you are a customer.

facts.statement: Fathom frames its business model as selling the software itself rather than selling visitor data, charging what it calls a fair price instead.

provenance.quote: If you aren't paying for the product, you are the product. That's why we charge a fair price for our software because we feel it's a more honest business model.

facts.statement: Fathom's dashboard is live/real-time, so a correct install can be confirmed by checking the 'Realtime' visitor count on the dashboard.

provenance.quote: Fathom's dashboard is live and real-time, so the best way to check if our script is installed is by visiting your website and seeing if your visit shows up in the "Realtime" count at the top of your dashboard.

facts.statement: Fathom is used by customers including Fortune 100 companies, banks and governments, alongside smaller companies.

provenance.quote: It's trusted by Fortune 100s, banks, governments and companies of every size.

facts.statement: Fathom is positioned primarily as a privacy-focused, cookieless replacement for Google Analytics for companies concerned with GDPR/EU privacy compliance.

entries.claim: EU isolation is enabled by default for every Fathom customer; there is nothing to set up.
entries.verbatim: If you want to use [EU isolation](https://usefathom.com/features/data-isolation), congratulations; as a Fathom customer, you’re already using it, and it’s enabled by default!

entries.claim: No setup, tweaking, or changes to the embed script are required to use EU isolation.
entries.verbatim: There’s nothing you have to set up or tweak or even change in [your embed script](/docs/script/embed) to use it.

entries.claim: Fathom automatically and intelligently routes data from EU visitors to be processed in the EU, and all other visitors' data to be processed in the US.
entries.verbatim: Fathom automatically and intelligently routes data from EU visitors to be processed in the EU and all other visitors to be processed in the US.

entries.claim: EU isolation also covers visitors from the non-EU-member nations Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom.
entries.verbatim: It includes visitors from the following non-eu member nations: - Iceland - Liechtenstein - Norway - Switzerland - United Kingdom

entries.claim: Fathom's EU servers are located in Falkenstein, Helsinki, and Nuremberg.
entries.verbatim: ### [Our EU server locations](#servers) - Falkenstein - Helsinki - Nuremberg

entries.claim: Customers who need all global traffic routed through the EU (Extreme EU Isolation) can use the script URL https://cdn-eu.usefathom.com/script.js instead of the default embed script.
entries.verbatim: If you need to use Extreme EU Isolation, where all global traffic is routed through the EU, please use `https://cdn-eu.usefathom.com/script.js` instead.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics Extreme EU Isolation
context.conditions: Requires loading the script from a different URL than the default embed script.

entries.claim: Firewall settings are adjusted by going to Settings, then Sites, clicking on the site, then clicking the Firewall tab.
entries.verbatim: To adjust your firewall settings, go to `Settings`, then `Sites`, click on your site, then click the `Firewall` tab.

entries.claim: The firewall offers separate list tabs for Pages, IPs, Referrers, Domains, Countries, and Events.
entries.verbatim: Open a list tab (Pages, IPs, Referrers, Domains, Countries, or Events).

entries.claim: Blocking pages, IPs, domains, or countries in the firewall does not prevent visitors from accessing or navigating the site; it only prevents their visits from being shown as data in the Fathom dashboard.
entries.verbatim: Note: If you've blocked pages, IPs, domains, or countries, visitors coming from those sources will still be able to access and navigate around your site, but their visits just won't be shown as data in your Fathom dashboard.

entries.claim: Pageviews from blocked pages do not count as pageviews and so do not count against the customer's payment plan allotment of pageviews.
entries.verbatim: Visitors who visit blocked pages do not count as pageviews, so they do not count against your payment plan allotment of pageviews.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics firewall - blocked pages
context.conditions: Applies to pages blocked via the firewall's Pages list.

entries.claim: Currently, only IPv4 addresses are supported for wildcard IP blocking in the firewall.
entries.verbatim: **Note:** Currently only IPv4 addresses are supported for wildcards

context.subject: Fathom Analytics firewall IP blocking
context.conditions: Applies to wildcard IP entries only.
context.limitations: IPv6 wildcard support not stated.

entries.claim: Once one or more allowed domains are added to the firewall's Domains list, data from any other domain is blocked instantly.
entries.verbatim: **Once you add one or more allowed domains, this means data coming from any other domain will be blocked instantly**.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics firewall domain allow list

entries.claim: In the Events firewall tab, Block drops the specified event names while still collecting every other event, Allow collects only the listed names and wildcard patterns, and an empty allow list collects every event.
entries.verbatim: **Block** drops those names and still collects every other event. **Allow** collects only the names (and wildcard patterns) on the list. An empty allow list collects every event.

entries.claim: The firewall only stops future visits; existing spam already recorded in reports must be removed separately using Data removals in the site's Manage settings.
entries.verbatim: The firewall stops future visits. To clean up spam that’s already in your reports, use `Data removals` in your site’s `Manage` settings.

entries.claim: An empty firewall list does not filter any traffic.
entries.verbatim: Choose `Block` or `Allow` the following values, then add them. An empty list does not filter.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics firewall lists
context.conditions: Applies to the Pages, IPs, Referrers, Domains, and Countries list tabs.

entries.claim: Fathom's tracking script can be installed via a WordPress plugin or one of Fathom's other integrations.
entries.verbatim: To start collecting data from your website, you need to [install our script](/docs/script/embed) in the header of your site’s code via our [WordPress plugin](/docs/integrations/wordpress) or using [one of our integrations](/docs/integrations)).

entries.claim: Fathom's dashboard is live and real-time, so installation can be verified by checking whether a visit appears in the Realtime count at the top of the dashboard.
entries.verbatim: Fathom’s dashboard is live and real-time, so the best way to check if our script is installed is by visiting your website and seeing if your visit shows up in the “Realtime” count at the top of your dashboard.

entries.claim: Excluding non-live environments (local, staging, or test) from Fathom also prevents those non-live pageviews from counting against the account's plan quota.
entries.verbatim: This also prevents non-live pageviews from counting against your plan quota.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics
context.conditions: Applies when local/staging/test environments are excluded via firewall settings.

entries.claim: Once allowed domains are set in the site firewall settings, Fathom filters out data from any hostname not on that list, including local, staging, and test domains.
entries.verbatim: Once allowed domains are set, Fathom filters out data from any hostname that is not on that list, including local, staging, and test domains.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics firewall - allowed domains
context.conditions: Requires adding the live website to allowed domains in site firewall settings.

entries.claim: IP address filtering to exclude staging/local visits works well for a single developer or a small, stable set of IP addresses, whereas allowed domains are more reliable for teams and changing networks.
entries.verbatim: This works well for a single developer or a small, stable set of IP addresses, but allowed domains are more reliable for teams and changing networks.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics firewall - IP filtering
context.conditions: Applies to excluding visits by IP address in firewall settings.
context.limitations: Vendor's own guidance on when each method is appropriate, not an independently measured comparison.

entries.claim: Fathom provides a browser console command, fathom.blockTrackingForMe();, run on a page where Fathom is installed, to block tracking in the current browser.
entries.verbatim: fathom.blockTrackingForMe();

context.subject: Fathom Analytics - browser console blocking
context.conditions: Run in the browser console on a page where the Fathom script is installed.

entries.claim: The browser-console tracking block set via fathom.blockTrackingForMe() is stored in the browser's local storage, so it keeps working for future visits from that browser.
entries.verbatim: This stores the setting in your browser’s local storage, so it will keep working for future visits from that browser.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics - browser console blocking
context.conditions: Follows use of fathom.blockTrackingForMe() in the browser console.

entries.verbatim: Fathom shows analytics in real time, so if the exclusion is working, your non-live visit should not show up as a current visitor.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics dashboard

objections.objection: Google Analytics is free and does more. Why would I start paying $15 a month for less?
objections.answer: The evidence meets this head-on rather than dodging it: there is deliberately no free plan, and the stated reason is infrastructure investment (E191, E192). The counter-frame is the business model — Fathom says it sells software, not data, and that free analytics are paid for with visitor data (E256, E193, E262, E151). Concretely: entry is $15/month for up to 100,000 pageviews across 50 sites (E157, E257), yearly billing gives two months free (E168), and the trial can run alongside Google Analytics so the comparison is empirical rather than rhetorical (E171). What the evidence does not do is claim feature parity with GA4, and copy should not either.

provenance.quote: Nope, and here’s why: we’ve invested heavily in fast, reliable infrastructure (we don’t host Fathom on cheap servers that go offline).

objections.objection: Switching means abandoning years of history, and I will lose the ability to compare this year with last year.
objections.answer: GA4 history can be imported, with no extra charge for historical imports, and the import is an authorise-select-run flow rather than a Google Cloud API key exercise (E42, E243, E74, E140). Imported history stays viewable and exportable while subscribed (E43), and Fathom's own retention is open-ended — data back to signup day for as long as you are a customer (E229, E69, E248, E145). Two honest limits belong in the same breath: the importer does not recreate every GA4 report and does not bring events (E44), and Universal Analytics data is gone because Google deleted it in July 2024 (E47).

objections.objection: The imported numbers will not match what Google showed me, so I will end up trusting neither tool.
objections.answer: Partially answerable, and only by saying it first: Fathom's own documentation states imported data has different filtering options and that totals can differ between tools (E45), and that large imports may need smaller date ranges (E46). The resolution on offer is parallel running during the trial so the reader calibrates the gap themselves rather than discovering it after switching (E171, E242), plus the reasons Fathom's counts differ by design — bot and crawler filtering (E122, E178) and no cookies or sampling-driven blind spots (E221, E90). There is no reconciliation report or mapping in the evidence.

provenance.quote: Imported data has different filtering options from data collected by Fathom, and the totals can differ between tools.

objections.objection: A single-page dashboard is too thin for how I work — I need funnels, cohorts, user-level paths, attribution across sessions and custom report building.
objections.answer: Nothing in the supplied evidence answers this, and that is the finding. The ceiling is explicit: one page of data (E76, E53) covering live and total visitors, pageviews, top pages, referrers, countries, devices, browsers, events and UTM campaigns, with filters, saved views, milestones and date comparisons. There is no funnel, cohort, session-path, multi-touch attribution or report-builder capability anywhere in the ledger, and Fathom frames the absence as the product's point rather than a roadmap gap. A reader who genuinely needs those should be allowed to disqualify themselves early; the Analytics API and CSV export (E179, E138, E139) are the only partial escape hatch, and they shift work onto the reader.

objections.objection: Seven days with my card on file is not long enough to judge an analytics tool, and I will forget to cancel.
objections.answer: The trial terms are documented and unusually explicit: card required, not charged until the trial ends, an email before billing starts, cancel anytime in account settings with no contracts and no call required (E170, E171, E185). Every plan includes the same features during the trial, so nothing is withheld (E169). Evaluation does not have to depend on the seven days alone — an eight-to-ten minute dashboard walkthrough and a clickable live demo exist without signing up (E190, E78, cta-live-demo), and the trial is designed to run alongside existing analytics (E171). Note the real residue: seven days of a low-traffic site is still a small sample, and nothing in the evidence extends it.

provenance.quote: Choose a plan and add your card to start a 7-day free trial. Your card is not charged until the trial ends, and we’ll email you before your plan starts billing. Your subscription then renews automatically unless you cancel in your account settings. You can run Fathom alongside your existing analytics while you try it.

objections.objection: Installing it means touching production templates and adding another script to a page I have spent weeks making fast.
objections.answer: Installation is one line of JavaScript in the header with the site's Site ID (E24, E242, E143, E27), or no template edits at all via the WordPress plugin and the other integrations — Ghost, Webflow, Next, Nuxt, Vue, Drupal, Carrd and more (E16, E103, E142, E244). Performance: a few KB, deferred and asynchronous, served from the nearest CDN edge, stated not to hurt PageSpeed (E80, E144, E222). Removing the cookie consent manager is itself a page-weight saving (E86, E227). Install can be confirmed in seconds by watching the Realtime count (E17), and staging or local traffic can be kept out via allowed domains, an IP filter or a browser-level block (E19, E20, E21, E22, E23).

objections.objection: Our security policy or hosting requirements mean we need to self-host analytics, or at minimum keep all data on our own infrastructure.
objections.answer: Nothing in the evidence answers this objection — it is a disqualifier. The documentation states plainly that Fathom is a hosted product only, with the trade-off being global CDN processing, fast dashboards and EU processing of EU visitor data. Copy should not attempt to argue around it; the nearest adjacent comfort available (EU routing, privacy-lawyer review, named enterprise logos) addresses data residency, not self-hosting, and a buyer whose constraint is literally on-premise will read any such pivot as evasion.

provenance.quote: No. Fathom is a hosted product so we can process pageviews on a global CDN, keep dashboards fast, and process EU visitor data in the EU.

objections.objection: I cannot get this past my team or procurement without a demo, a security review and someone on a call — and they explicitly do not do sales calls.
objections.answer: Only partly answerable. Fathom states outright that it does no sales calls or live demos, offering instead a ten-minute walkthrough video, a clickable live dashboard and the trial (E190), plus email support from real humans on every plan (E181, cta-contact-support). For internal credibility: privacy lawyers have vetted collection and storage (E120), EU traffic routes through European-owned infrastructure under Canada's EU adequacy decision (E219, E34), compliance with GDPR, ePrivacy, PECR and CCPA is claimed (E116-E119, E220), and the customer base is described as including Fortune 100s, banks, governments and Premier League clubs, with named logos (E230, E258, E231). Be precise about what is missing: no named certifying body, no audit report, no SOC 2 or ISO reference anywhere in the evidence, and the logos are logo placements with no usage detail. A procurement process that requires an attestation will not be satisfied by this material.

provenance.quote: We don’t do sales calls or live demos, but our software is ridiculously easy to use. You can watch our [10-minute walkthrough](/video/dashboard-walkthrough), click around the [live dashboard](https://app.usefathom.com/demo) or give Fathom a 7-day free trial alongside your existing analytics.

objections.objection: If I am leaving Google anyway, Cloudflare's analytics are free and I could self-host Matomo or Plausible — why pay this one?
objections.answer: The evidence engages this as a comparison rather than denying it. Cloudflare's privacy-first analytics are acknowledged as free (E99, E100); the counter is paid-product consequences, not feature claims. Against Matomo specifically: cloud retention capped at 24 months versus retention for as long as you are a customer (E68, E69); cookies and consent notices unless several steps are taken correctly, versus anonymisation and no cookies by default (E87, E88, E89, E90, E91, E92, E66); a GA import needing a Google Cloud API key versus a button (E73, E74); a 20-50KB script you must put behind your own CDN versus a few KB on Fathom's (E82, E83, E80); 12 sections and 70+ reports versus one page (E75, E76). Against self-hosting generally, Fathom's position is that it is hosted so there is no infrastructure to run (E148, E192). All of the Matomo points are Fathom's own comparison claims, not independent verification (E60, E63, E68), and must be attributed as such.

provenance.quote: They offer privacy-first, lightweight and simple website analytics—and their analytics are free.

objections.objection: My traffic is spiky. One post that takes off and I am either throttled, surprise-billed or forced up a tier I do not need the rest of the year.
objections.answer: Documented and generous: occasional spikes are never charged for and the account is not shut off on hitting the limit early (E253); staying well over the limit triggers an email about a larger plan with the decision left to the customer, friendly reminders and extra time before dashboard and API access pauses, and data keeps being collected throughout (E186, E254, E255). Downgrading is self-serve after two consecutive months under the tier (E189). Quota hygiene is in the customer's hands: blocked pages and excluded local, staging or test environments do not count against the allotment (E10, E18), and bots are filtered automatically (E122, E178). Two caveats to state rather than hide: custom events count against the same monthly allowance (E187, E183), and sites on one plan share it (E247).

provenance.quote: We’ll never turn your analytics off for occasional traffic spikes. If you stay well over your limit, we’ll email you about a larger plan, and you decide whether to upgrade or cancel (no hard feelings either way). We send a few friendly reminders and extra time before we pause dashboard and API access, and we keep collecting your data throughout.

objections.objection: It is two bootstrapped founders with no funding. If they fold or get acquired, my analytics history goes with them.
objections.answer: Thinly answerable. Independence is stated as a feature — no venture capital, bank loans or outside shareholders, and pricing set to be sustainable because the business model is software rather than data (E245, E193, E256); the company has been running since 2018 (E61, E101). Data is exportable at any time as CSV or through the API, and Fathom tells customers to export before cancelling because cancellation queues data for deletion (E138, E139, E250, E70, E185). What the evidence does not contain: revenue, headcount, uptime history or any continuity commitment, and 'thousands of companies' and the logo wall are unquantified vendor statements (E213, E215, E231). Do not dress bootstrapped independence up as a durability guarantee.

This map compares captured claims from the pages read, not complete product capabilities. Unread pages and extraction omissions remain unknown. Open ground is a hypothesis to verify, never proof of exclusivity or of a rival's inability.

**Shared category vocabulary.** Two or more competitors use these. Keep the words needed to explain the product; common vocabulary alone does not make a proposition generic. Avoid unsupported superlatives:
- analytics, data, free, per, reports, day, events, like, offers, see, tracking, via, card, collection, complete, consent

Current product knowledge is compared with saved competitor pages; check their capture dates before making time-sensitive comparisons.

**Supported product propositions.** Use their stated conditions. An unmatched capture is a question to verify, not exclusivity.

profiles.name: Plausible Analytics
profiles.why: Both Plausible and Fathom position themselves as privacy-first, cookieless Google Analytics alternatives with a built-in GA import path—Plausible says 'You can even import your Google Analytics stats' while Fathom's importer requires only authorizing the account, selecting sites and running the import (E74). Plausible markets itself as explicitly EU-hosted, with visitor data processed 'exclusively on servers owned and operated by European companies,' whereas Fathom instead claims its 'intelligent routing' makes its script load 'up to 50% faster than EU-only infrastructure' (E105), treating EU-only hosting as a benchmark to beat rather than a selling point in itself.
profiles.discovery_reason: The closest like-for-like swap buyers compare against when picking a cookieless, EU-friendly analytics tool with a simple dashboard and open-source option.
profiles.one_liner: Easy to use and privacy-friendly Google Analytics alternative
profiles.promise: Plausible is powerful, lightweight analytics. No cookies, just insights. Made and hosted in the EU, powered by European-owned infrastructure.
profiles.pricing: Usage-tiered by monthly pageviews (shown at the 10k tier): Starter $9/month (one site, 3-year retention), Growth $14/month (up to 3 sites, 3 team members), Business $19/month (up to 10 sites, 10 team members, Stats API); Enterprise is custom/contact sales for 10+ sites. Annual billing offers 2 months free versus monthly billing.
profiles.free_entry: 30-day free trial, no credit card required (https://plausible.io/); open-source code available on GitHub.
profiles.icp: Site owners for whom 'Google Analytics is overkill' and who want insights 'without complexity, training or prior analytics experience.'

profiles.name: Simple Analytics
profiles.why: Both position themselves as GDPR-compliant, privacy-first analytics: Fathom says it is "GDPR, ePrivacy, PECR and CCPA compliant" (E116), while Simple Analytics says it "is GDPR compliant from installation" and that data is "stored in the EU, with our primary infrastructure in the Netherlands." Simple Analytics' own pages frame the product mainly around running alongside GA4 to capture consent-rejected traffic, a different emphasis from Fathom's GDPR-as-controller framing, so the discovery hypothesis's description of an equivalent minimal EU-hosted dashboard only partly matches what these pages promise.
profiles.discovery_reason: Buyers comparing privacy-first, no-personal-data analytics tools put this alongside Fathom for its similarly minimal, EU-hosted dashboard.

profiles.name: Umami
profiles.why: Umami states it 'is open-source and can be self-hosted for free,' giving developers full infrastructure control, while our evidence shows Fathom is hosted-only ('Fathom is a hosted product so we can process pageviews on a global CDN') and starts at $15/month for up to 100,000 monthly pageviews. Both vendors let customers keep and export their analytics data, but Fathom's ownership guarantee holds only 'as long as you're a customer,' whereas Umami's self-host option removes that dependency on continued payment entirely.
profiles.discovery_reason: Developers who are price-sensitive or want full data control look here as the self-hosted, open-source route instead of paying a monthly SaaS fee.

profiles.name: Matomo
profiles.why: Matomo's homepage lists Funnels & Flows, Heatmaps & recordings, and A/B testing & personalisation as core capabilities, which supports the hypothesis that teams wanting more depth than Fathom's simple stats evaluate Matomo; both vendors assert GDPR compliance (Fathom: E116, E117, E118; Matomo: 'Protect user privacy and stay compliant with GDPR and other regulations without sacrificing insight' on https://matomo.org/), so privacy compliance itself is a documented overlap rather than a differentiator. This reflects a documented difference in advertised feature breadth, not evidence that Fathom lacks these capabilities or that any buyer has switched.
profiles.discovery_reason: Teams that need more depth than Fathom's simple stats (funnels, heatmaps, cohorts) but still want privacy-respecting, GDPR-focused tracking end up evaluating this.
profiles.promise: Matomo delivers accurate, GDPR-compliant analytics with full data ownership in a platform teams can set up in minutes.
profiles.pricing: Cloud Business plan starts at $29/month (excl. tax) at the lowest published traffic tier (50,000 hits/month), with higher named tiers up to 'More than 10 million hits per month'; annual billing gives 2 months free ('Get 2 months free with annual billing!'). Above 10 million hits/month, Matomo says 'Contact us for tracking more than 10 million hits per month. Matomo Cloud can scale to hundreds of millions of hits per month.' Cloud Enterprise and On-Premise Enterprise are custom-priced ('Contact us for custom pricing and allowances').
profiles.free_entry: Start a 21-day free Cloud trial, or self-host forever for free. Full access to all features. No credit card required.
profiles.icp: Organisations wanting accurate, GDPR-compliant analytics with full data ownership, described as 'Built for teams, not experts'; named industries include Banks, Enterprise, Financial Institutions, and Fintech, and the site claims trust 'from enterprises to public sector leader'.

map.summary: 7 audience(s) mapped; 0 worth exploring first. Commercial priority is a hypothesis, not a response-rate forecast.
map.validation_note: Checked 9 pages; 1 fetch failure(s). Quotes are source-verified; interpretations and purchase intent are hypotheses.
map.reading:
Assessment summary. Verified quotations do not establish demand or purchase intent; commercial priority remains a hypothesis.
- A technical founder who built the site himself and gave up on GA4 somewhere around the third Explore report: review first; product compatibility supported; audience evidence supported (6 quoted source(s)); use or purchase captured; reachability venue identified.
- The person at a European company who has been told, by someone with authority, that Google Analytics has to go: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence limited (3 quoted source(s)); use or purchase unknown; reachability venue identified.
- A clinic group or telehealth startup rebuilding its public marketing site after the tracking-pixel settlements: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence limited (1 quoted source(s)); use or purchase unknown; reachability venue identified.
- A small nonprofit or advocacy site whose visitors would be endangered by ad-tech trackers: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence limited (2 quoted source(s)); use or purchase unknown; reachability venue identified.
- A freelancer or small studio who installs analytics on every client site and gets asked for the numbers by people who will never log in: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence absent (1 quoted source(s)); use or purchase unknown; reachability venue identified.
- A US business that just received a CIPA 'wiretapping' demand letter naming the scripts on its website: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence limited (1 quoted source(s)); use or purchase unknown; reachability unknown.
- A small EU-selling ecommerce brand whose consent banner is eating a third of its own sales data: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence limited (3 quoted source(s)); use or purchase unknown; reachability unknown.
map.note: Coverage gaps and failures: (1) Direct buyer-voice forum threads were hard to surface — three attempts at Reddit and Hacker News practitioner threads on freelance multi-client analytics and Ghost/newsletter publishers returned vendor comparison pages instead, so the freelancer segment leans on the existence of a reporting-tool market rather than quoted complaints. (2) No churn evidence found: searches for people who left or cancelled Fathom turned up only review-site remarks that it is 'expensive for what you get' and costs more per pageview than Plausible past 1M views, with no first-person account — real churn reasons remain unknown. (3) Security posture unverified: a search for Fathom Analytics SOC 2/BAA returned results for an unrelated AI meeting-notes company also called Fathom, so treat any certification claim as unconfirmed and do not reuse those hits. (4) No named EU public-sector or university procurement decision was found, so the institutional variant of the compliance buyer is unsupported and was not proposed as a separate segment. (5) Search scope was left empty, so no geography was imposed; German-language vocabulary was tried once and returned agency listicles rather than buyer discussion. (6) Population counts are unknown throughout, fit is left at zero, and assessment fields are left at defaults for separate validation. (7) The Shopify candidate has no documented install path in the supplied capability catalogue — verify before using it. (8) One source (clickport) is a vendor-adjacent guide and one (levelup) is a practitioner essay; both should be read as advocacy, and the consent-loss percentages they cite differ widely and need independent checking.

segments.name: A technical founder who built the site himself and gave up on GA4 somewhere around the third Explore report
segments.organization: Bootstrapped software company or indie SaaS, 1-10 people, where the founder also owns the marketing site, docs and changelog (self-deployed Next/Nuxt/Laravel/Ghost stack)
segments.workflow: Ships a feature or writes a launch post, then wants to see within seconds which page or link brought signups; today that means opening GA4, landing in report configuration, and closing the tab unanswered
segments.need: A one-screen read on whether this week's shipping brought anyone, with no consent banner in front of his own launch page and no analytics administration
segments.buyer_role: Founder (same person signs up and pays on a card, self-serve)
segments.current_alternative: GA4 left installed by inertia, sometimes alongside a cookie consent manager; free self-hosted options (GoatCounter, Umami, Plausible CE) are the live competing choice in this crowd

counterevidence_summary: Technically literate site owners in this crowd default to free hosted or self-hosted analytics when volume is low and the site is non-commercial. — A no-cost substitute that satisfies the same 'is anyone reading this' need directly competes with a paid subscription that has no free plan. Review before prioritising.

The no-consent-banner argument is openly contested in this audience on ePrivacy grounds, so it cannot be assumed to close the sale. — For this segment the dominant stated driver is GA's complexity and distrust, not banner removal, so a disputed banner claim is an argument to avoid rather than a blocker. Minor condition; does not exclude this audience.
reasons: OpenCage — a small, founder-run geocoding API business whose engineer writes the stack posts — publicly documents stopping Google Analytics and paying for Fathom, which is both usage and a stated paid relationship from a member of this exact segment.
The stated reasons match the candidate's hypothesised need almost word for word: GA grew too complex, and a single page answering basic questions was the deciding feature.

Product truth supplies every required capability for this workflow: one-line header install (fact_7dd83c7d9d826647), single-page dashboard (fact_5a6a507e2ebb14bd), real-time install verification (fact_db7edad49bb507cf), never uses cookies (fact_213fb3b9ea5024ba), framework integrations (fact_27803407292d4b6d), and running alongside existing analytics during a trial (fact_cd04dd2d3fd37001).
Hacker News is a verified public venue where this audience discusses and compares analytics tooling.
Re-ranked on matching researched sources (10 fetched).
unknowns: The captured purchase dates from 2018 and was partly justified by open-source/self-host optionality that the current hosted-only product no longer offers; whether today's version of this buyer still converts is untested.
No evidence in the corpus about how many such founders pay versus install a free tool.
Nothing in the corpus about install-to-first-insight time or about funnel/cohort needs surfacing after the switch.
1 unsupported or duplicate quotation(s) discarded.
Review the counterevidence before prioritising this audience.

research.audience_name: A technical founder who built the site himself and gave up on GA4 somewhere around the third Explore report

required_structural_signals.description: Founder-operated software company or solo product business
Marketing site, docs or blog deployed by the founder, not by an outside agency

required_workflow_signals.description: An analytics script is already live on the site
No analytics team or data owner between the founder and the tag
Changelog, blog or launch posts published regularly enough to need real-time reads

hard_disqualifiers.description: Fathom is hosted only
Single-page dashboard; no funnel, cohort or session-path capability in the catalogue
No free plan; card required for the 7-day trial

situation.text: The corpus shows individuals who personally built and ran their own blog, portfolio, or small-company site, who had installed Google Analytics (in some cases later GA4) by default, and who at some point found the tool too complex or confusing for the simple traffic questions they actually had, prompting them to look for or switch to a simpler alternative.

evidence.quote: For me, it is important to see analytics about my portfolio website. This way, I can see which posts got the most views, which country my users are from, and which browser & operating system they are using.
When starting my blog, I integrated Google Analytics — it's free, easy to set up (just drop a few tags on the page), and that's what I knew back then.

I am kind of confused what GA4 is offering. All I want to see: - Real time visitors - Keywords bringing people on my site - Basic Reporting for # of Views monthly/yearly basis. Is there any free alternative?
A few days ago we stopped using Google analytics on our site. We now instead use Fathom Analytics.

situation.inference_basis: Combines separate first-person accounts: people who built and run their own small sites (S7, S8), and separately people who found Google Analytics/GA4 too complex or confusing for their needs (S3, S1). No single quoted source states both facts together, and none of the sources describe a company founder specifically or a launch-triggered reporting failure.

problems.statement: Google Analytics (and, for at least one buyer, GA4 specifically) is reported as too complex or confusing to quickly answer simple traffic questions, pushing some site owners toward simpler alternatives.

evidence.quote: Google analytics has just gotten increasingly complex over time. Frankly it gets harder and harder to understand, and more and more of a slog to wade through. I kept finding myself lost in sub-menu 27 when all I wanted was basic information.

I am kind of confused what GA4 is offering. All I want to see: - Real time visitors - Keywords bringing people on my site - Basic Reporting for # of Views monthly/yearly basis. Is there any free alternative?

Looking for web analytics tools that are not Google Analytics and are user-friendly, not highly technical like Mixpanel and let you keep track of the basics - How many users? Where do they come from? Etc
It was overkill for my use case:Google Analytics is overkill for most website owners. It’s a powerful but complex tool that can take time to understand and requires training.

problems.statement: Running Google Analytics (or similar cookie-based trackers) is associated with needing cookie/GDPR/CCPA consent banners, which at least one buyer described as an annoying and widespread cost to visitor experience, and which motivated choosing cookie-less tools.

evidence.quote: To abide by the privacy regulations, you compromise your visitors experience by displaying annoying cookie banners and GDPR or CCPA consent notices. This is the case of many websites nowadays.
No cookies, so I don't have to worry about GDPR banners or whatever
